title: UX Career Paths Are Weird
intro: A straightforward UX career path is a myth. The most experienced practitioners got there through unexpected combinations of roles and industries.

learn.title: A scribbly line
learn.text:
Calabro's own path: **ARRIS** (behavioural UX design at a telecom company, before “UX” was a job title) → **Minitab** (nine years beside PhD statisticians) → **Siemens Software** (building ResearchOps at enterprise scale) → consulting and generative research → **FINRA** (research inside a large, complex regulated environment).

“Not A to B, but a scribbly line with a series of short stints at drastically different organisations.”

try.q: What did nine years beside PhD statisticians give him?
options: Quantitative reasoning no UX course teaches
A formal statistics qualification from a university
try.explain: It's what made him a mixed-methods researcher.

learn.title: The pressure to look linear
learn.text:
The pressure to have a **clean career narrative** works against developing the breadth that makes researchers effective.

A zig-zag isn't a failure to commit. It's how someone ends up able to run a usability test, size the result, build the ops to repeat it, and explain the money to an executive.

try.q: What does the pressure for a clean narrative cost?
options: The breadth that makes researchers effective
Time that could be spent developing one deep specialism
try.explain: Linear stories reward depth in one place and punish range.

learn.title: Why he published it
learn.text:
“Sharing a messy path helps to take some of the pressure off the rest of you.”

The point isn't that everyone should job-hop. It's that the combination you end up with matters more than the shape of the line — and that unexpected depth (statistics, operations, a regulated industry) is often what makes someone valuable later.

try.q: What does the article say matters more than the shape of the path?
options: The combination of skills you end up with
How quickly you specialise in a single research method

test.explain: Before UX was commonly used as a job title.

test.q: What did he build at Siemens?
options: A quantitative research team working with statisticians
test.explain: Operations infrastructure for a large organisation.

test.q: What is the article's view of short stints?
options: They should be hidden on a CV
test.explain: Drastically different organisations taught different things.

test.q: What is “unexpected depth” in this context?
options: Expertise picked up outside the UX syllabus
Deep knowledge of one product over many years

test.q: Why did he share his own path?
options: To take pressure off people with messy paths
To argue for frequent job changes
To document how UX job titles have changed over time
test.explain: The article is reassurance, not advice to move.
